Thousands of known phishing domains, updated every day and checked on your phone. No link you scan is sent anywhere for this.

Spots fake and look-alike sites, letters from other alphabets, hidden IP addresses, short links and other tricks.
Recognizes pressure, prize, payment and password requests in 9 languages.
Checks links in incoming notifications and warns you before you tap them (optional).
Analysis runs on your device. Online lookups are off unless you turn them on.
Flags premium-rate and satellite numbers, foreign or invalid IBANs and crypto wallet addresses in messages.
Scan a QR code with the camera, or share a picture of one. The hidden link is checked before you open it.
Tell us about a false alarm or a missed scam through a public GitHub form. Your message text is never included.
A 0–100 risk score, every warning sign explained, and what to do next.
Reads text in screenshots on your device and checks the links in them.
Share a link, a message or a file from any app, or choose TrustCheck when opening a link. Links are never opened automatically.
No warning signs were found in this file. This does not prove the file is harmless.
This file shows warning signs typical of malware or scams.
Opens VirusTotal in your browser. Only the file\'s SHA-256 fingerprint is shared, not the file.
TrustCheck looks for warning signs; it is not an antivirus and cannot prove a file is harmless.
All scan history on this device will be permanently deleted.
The app can read the screen and act on your behalf. Banking trojans abuse this.
The app can become a device admin, which makes it hard to uninstall.
The app is named after a well-known brand, but its package does not belong to that brand.
The app is signed with Android\'s public test key, which official apps never use.
The app can ask to install further apps.
The app can read all notifications, including verification codes.
The app can cover other apps, for example with a fake login screen.
The app asks to read or send text messages, which can be used to steal verification codes.
SMS access combined with screen control or overlays is a typical pattern of banking malware.
This domain appears in the threat feed synced to your device.
A well-known brand name is combined with other words in a domain the brand does not own.
A brand name is placed at the start of an unrelated domain to look official.
The message asks for login details, verification codes or card data.
The message asks for payment to a crypto wallet. Such payments cannot be reversed and are common in scams.
This link can run code or embed content instead of opening a normal website.
The name ends like a document or photo but is really an app or program (e.g. invoice.pdf.apk).
The link carries another web address that you may be forwarded to.
Many encoded characters can be used to hide the real destination.
The link points to an installable file. Install apps only from trusted stores.
This file can install or run software. Open it only if you trust where it came from.
The file\'s content does not match its name: it is an app or program pretending to be something else.
A link inside this file shows warning signs. Its own report is in your history.
The IBAN belongs to a bank in another country. Local companies rarely ask for payment to a foreign account.
The number is registered in another country. Be careful if the message claims to come from a local company.
Imitates a brand with look-alike letters
Letters from another alphabet are used to imitate a well-known brand.
The link uses HTTP, so data you send is not encrypted.
Domains with many hyphens are often generated for scams.
This number belongs to a global satellite or network service. Calling it is usually very expensive.
The IBAN fails its checksum, so it was mistyped or made up. Do not send money to it.
IP address instead of a name
Legitimate services rarely send links that use a bare IP address.
Words like login, verify or account are common in phishing links.
Very long links can hide the real destination.
The domain closely resembles a well-known brand but is not owned by it.
Macros in Office documents can run code. Do not enable them for unexpected files.
The domain mixes Latin letters with letters from another alphabet that look the same.
The address is written in an unusual numeric form to hide where it points.
The message asks for a fee, payment, gift card or cryptocurrency.
The link uses a non-standard network port.
Calls or texts to this number can cost a lot per minute. Scammers use such numbers to charge victims.
The link points to a device on a local network, such as a router.
The message promises a prize, gift or easy money.
The domain uses non-Latin characters. This is normal for many sites but can also be abused.
The link passes through many redirects before reaching its destination.
The short link forwards you to a different domain.
Scripts can run commands on a computer. They are a common way to spread malware.
The link contains fields such as a password or PIN.
Short links hide their real destination.
Long chains of subdomains are used to make addresses look official.
A threat-intelligence service lists this link as phishing or malware.
This domain ending is often used in abuse reports. This alone is a weak signal.
The message tries to rush you, for example with threats of account suspension.
Text before the @ sign is ignored by browsers; the real site comes after it.
The domain is written with letters from another alphabet that imitate Latin letters.

Your history stays on this device and contains only link addresses, file names and results — never your messages or file contents. You can delete it at any time. Every feature is free; Premium only removes ads.
Every feature below is free for everyone.
TrustCheck downloads a list of known phishing domains once a day from its GitHub project (on Wi-Fi when possible) and checks links against it on your phone. Nothing you scan is uploaded.
Checks run on your phone first and work offline. TrustCheck looks at the link, the message and the file itself, and compares links with a threat list that is updated every day.
All permissions are optional. You can change them later in Settings.
To warn you automatically, TrustCheck needs permission to read notification text. Text is processed in memory to find links and is never stored or uploaded.
Lets TrustCheck find links in incoming messages and warn you before you tap them.
Lets TrustCheck show a warning when it finds a dangerous link.
TrustCheck helps you spot phishing links, scam messages and malicious websites before they can harm you.
